Although the planets are not yet fully formed, given their estimated ages of around $660$ million years, transit photometry indicates the masses of the planets to be $\sim0.24$, $\sim0.39$, and $\sim0.41$ times the mass of Jupiter, yielding minimum densities of $\sim

This research focuses on the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen-doped TiO2 to improve high-temperature superconductivity materials. Carbon and nitrogen atoms were substituted at various Ti and oxygen sites within the TiO2 crystal lattice, and five distinct superconducting phases were found for both types of dopants. Notably, these phases can be grouped based on the distribution of carbon and nitrogen atoms: like-doping and alternate-doping patterns. In contrast to previous studies, our calculations incorporated both spin-polarized and spin-unpolarized states to fully explore this multi-framework. Depending on doping pattern and location, materials exhibited either half-metallic or metallic behavior. Specifically, like-doping patterns displayed metallic characteristics in all TiO2 cases, whereas alternate-doping displayed half-metallic behavior. Interestingly, an anti-ferromagnetic order was observed in N-doped Ti(4a) like-doping pattern, indicating potential for novel applications. Our study provides a detailed electronic and magnetic landscape, paving the way for further investigation into high-temperature superconductivity in C,N-doped TiO2.

The characteristics of top quarks make their production in diagonal $q t \bar{t}$ pairs at a hadron collider extremely difficult to detect due to the difficulty in identifying and measuring one of the quarks that decays into a lepton and neutrino. A novel strategy called "Elastic Energy" is suggested to overcome this challenge and identify the presence of heavy particles such as the Standard Model's Higgs boson or any new resonances based on the conservation of momentum. This method utilizes the fact that in quark scattering where the other quark remains undetected, the top quark or the resonance decays into a set of particles that allow for inference of their identity and mass through analysis of their decay products and a single missing neutrino. This technique could potentially be applied to detect the elastic production of the Higgs boson at the LHC with an expected minimum of about 100 ab$^{-1}$, or any future hadron collider, requiring very little information about the initial state's transverse momentum.

Our investigation continues in the context of the intra-cluster medium, focusing on using statistical measures like structure functions to detect turbulent eddies via sulfur-sodium asymmetries observed by X-rays. However, accurately measuring these eddies is complicated due to limited and imprecise X-ray spectroscopic data. Moreover, linear components alone cannot fully describe the structure functions, as they exhibit non-zero skewness at various scales. This study builds upon the previous investigation and delves deeper into ambiguities arising from measurement errors, non-Gaussian fluctuations, and spatially varying mean densities when analyzing structure functions. A new method is proposed to differentiate between these factors and estimate the parameters of eddy-generated turbulence. Utilizing mock X-ray spectra, we found that a two-component fit to the reduced structure functions can provide reliable eddy parameter estimates. Notably, these findings are robust against fluctuations in gas density fluctuations and can be applied to a range of cosmological scenarios.

Upcoming work by Monkhamsadov and Panagiotis (2023) examines the concept of Ramsey upper richness for infinite graph families that can be colored differently, drawing a parallel to another property already studied by researchers. We expand on this concept by also looking at infinite graphs that have a specific coloring property, already studied by researchers, and also explore how this upper richness relates to another property known as Fulkersonness for specific graphs like complete bipartite graphs and tripartite complete graphs. Our work also proves several key theorems related to these graphs and demonstrates the infinite graph version of a related conjecture.

The complex structure within the Central Molecular Zone of the Milky Way remains poorly understood, particularly in terms of its 3D shape formations. Recent research has focused on its possible elongated form along the galactic plane, yet ANTZEDGE offers a novel statistical approach to analyze its intricate, possibly anisotropic, spatial configurations. By employing a 2D correlation function, this study aims to understand the three-dimensional density framework of the CMZ through spatial correlations within its stellar population. Utilizing near-infrared spectroscopic data from over 3000 stars within the region, our three-dimensional density framework illuminates the three-dimensional density framework of the CMZ through a novel metric called excess density, revealing its three-dimensional density framework within various height layers above and below the galactic plane. Our research indicates that the CMZ's density framework exhibits a two-arm structure in its central regions and broader extensions towards its sides, exhibiting elliptical and parabolic cross-sections respectively. Additionally, our analysis suggests that elongation in the CMZ's density framework is most pronounced in its central regions and less so in its broader extensions.

This paper introduces a novel approach to identifying Bell's Palsy solely through eye asymmetry in video footage, innovating by focusing analysis on eye movements and variations rather than adopting a face-centered method. This innovative technique is uniquely capable of working with low-resolution or cropped videos, and can effectively detect the disorder even when only a person's eyes are visible. Our proposed solution leverages both traditional hand-crafted features and state-of-the-art deep learning models to maximize accuracy. Experimental results demonstrate superior performance compared to existing face-centered methods, particularly in scenarios involving low-resolution videos, and reveal a significant 5% accuracy improvement in videos with low frame rates. Our dataset, consisting of 1600 video clips collected from 200 healthy subjects, along with comprehensive evaluation outcomes, are publicly accessible for research purposes.

Our analysis focuses on the scalar quantum electrodynamics in two dimensions, an often-used model for studying phase transitions and critical phenomena. We considered three scenarios: quasi-equilibrium, steady-state, and time-dependent dynamics following a sudden change. By employing a qudit-based approach, we considered two methods for creating these scenarios: sudden creation of interactions and sudden expansion of the system. Our findings show that noise, intentionally added, can enhance the stabilization of non-classical states, an increase in system bath coupling leads to the enhancement of certain correlations and local field non-Gaussian behavior in the case of sudden creation of interactions; however, this finding does not apply to sudden expansions where increased noise results in the suppression of oscillations and provides damping effects similar to those caused by an entanglement growing medium. Our study's open hardware design allows for the investigation of other models and scenarios.

In our investigation, we simulate the interaction between highly intense polarized laser pulses and metallic surfaces, and we find that these surfaces can significantly enhance the production of polarized positron-pair particles. By utilizing polarized laser pulses in the X-ray range and irradiating them on negatively charged graphsene sheets, we observe a notable increase in pair-production efficiency compared to traditional targets. Our calculations and simulations, validated against the COMPOSITE code, demonstrate nearly 100% linear polarization in the generated pairs as a function of energy, providing a potential pathway for producing highly intense, polarized positron beams in the future.

A subgroup $H$ of a group $G$ is considered wide if it contains a subgroup $K$ such that $G$ is the union of conjugates of $K$. The subgroup width is defined as the minimum entropy among all wide subgroups. In this study, we identify the structure of finite groups with low subgroup width, specifically finding that groups with a low subgroup width have a large normal subgroup and a specific composition of simple groups. Consequently, we discover that a sufficiently large probability mass exists on elements that are not symmetries in some subgroup with low entropy. This result has implications for the rapid mixing of random walks on certain types of groups.

This research details an innovative temperature sensing system tailored for low-power and voltage-restricted applications. The proposed circuit uses a compact and cost-effective design, prioritizing suitability over high precision. It is capable of securely converting raw data into three distinct temperature ranges corresponding to cold, comfortable, and hot sensations without requiring a microcontroller or software support. The circuit's voltage compliance extends from 0.6V to 1.8V, and it operates effectively across a wide temperature spectrum (-40{\deg}C to 85{\deg}C) with a low supply current of 74\mu A at 3.3V. Furthermore, the circuit features a user-adjustable sensitivity knob, enabling the customization of the temperature detection sensitivity to a specific application's requirements.

We analyze the long-term behavior of solutions to the 3D stellar momentum equations under specific conditions. These conditions involve a steady-state, axisymmetric magnetic field with pressure and density that vary only radially, all within a star assumed to be incompressible and confined within R. The focus of the study lies in N-shaped profiles, which significantly enhance robust stability proofs across the full range of the domain 'R', thus eliminating the need to use a scaled-down model (torus). This stability holds for any initial conditions and demonstrates that the system's energy decays exponentially over time outside the boundary layer, with a smooth axisymmetric component and pressure that also decline at an exponential rate. The overall stability in R is achieved by combining the exponential boundary layer stability (found in prior works) with the new outside boundary layer decay (a recent breakthrough). Notably, the newly discovered outside boundary layer decay shares the mathematical framework of related studies on pressure and density in rotating fluid dynamics.

The functional renormalization group (FRG) technique has become a key numerical and non-perturbative tool in quantum field theory that enables researchers to solve complex models by approximating the Renormalized Coupling Constant (RCC) curve as a function of the regulator scale. Due to its versatility, the FRG approach has been successfully applied to various quantum field theories, from simple models to complex systems involving turbulence and superconductivity. In this paper, we introduce an open-source FRG framework designed to solve quantum field theories in a variety of dimensions and theories, and we demonstrate its utility with the O(N) model in multiple dimensions. By plugging in different ansatzes for the Renormalization Group Flow of the RCC curve, we obtain and compare the post-flow RCC curves for multiple scenarios, and we investigate the implications of our findings, particularly in the context of critical phenomena and phase transitions. Additionally, we discuss the potential for this framework to facilitate research collaborations and further exploration of quantum field theories using the FRG approach.

A music generation task, often called the "Pied Piper" test, demands that an artificial neural network be able to match or surpass the ability of a human composer. Evaluating this ability requires creating music that is not only sonically appealing but also aligns with stylistic expectations of a specific genre. However, current datasets used for assessment are limited in size and diversity. To address this shortcoming, we introduce the P2Mu corpus, a comprehensive dataset comprising 500 pieces of music across five distinct styles from the Virtual Reality platform Meta Quest. Evaluators ranked the samples based on their creativity, appeal, and genre consistency, resulting in the selection of 144 samples that can serve as a reliable benchmark for evaluating networks on the Pied Piper test across multiple genres.

This working paper explores various structural elements within Lie groupoids and differentiable stacks, focusing on elements such as connections, torsions, principal bundles, connections on stacks, Caliber systems, and Cerf functions. We can trace a recurring pattern that involves translating properties of a Lie group or differential manifold to a Lie groupoid or differentiable stack. Each case within this analysis includes an associated example with a corresponding calculation.

A comprehensive observation of the Dragon infrared dark cloud (IRDC) has been carried out using the Dragon1 molecular outposts, which are essential components for understanding the dynamics of the core. A unique feature of this region is its exceptionally high opacity, making it an ideal setting for studying the early stages of molecular cloud evolution. By analyzing the spectral energy distribution (SED) and spectral lines, a significant discrepancy has been identified in the estimated mass of the region, indicating a substantial amount of unseen matter. Analysis of the regional dynamics has also led to an calculation of a significantly lower mass requirement for gravitational stability than what is observed, further highlighting the discrepancy. By comparing the surface density of the region to that of other similar formations, it is evident that the region exhibits an exceptional level of gravitational condensation. These findings suggest a significant amount of potential mass within the region, which may be essential for the formation of a disk around a central star. As a result, our analysis suggests that a significant amount of hidden mass may be essential for the process of stellar formation.

Godel modal logics can be viewed as extensions of intutionistic logic that incorporate operators representing necessity and possibility. This paper explores the relationships between various algebras and relational structures for a range of Godel modal logics. Specifically, we focus on Godel modal logics constructed from underlying Finitary Finite Varieties (FFRVs) of relational structures. In this context, we define a corresponding algebraic system with necessity and possibility operators for each FFRV of relational structures, denoted as $\sigma$-Godel modal algebra. Additionally, we establish a foundational relational system, or frame, for each FFRV of relational structures, equipped with necessity and possibility modal operators, and establish the principles that govern these systems. It is proven that every algebra of this type is equivalent to a frame within this system. The relationships between Godel modal algebras and their frame counterparts can be described by a series of Brouwer-Heyting-Kleene equational axioms expanded to include modal operators, specifically $\sigma$-BHKs. The infinitary extensions of these frame theories, denoted as $\sigma$-BHKs, allow for characterizations of all Godel modal algebras constructed from algebras belonging to FFRV of relational structures, and certain subvarieties of these structures.

LiDAR point clouds offer valuable, high-precision spatial information for pinpointing objects and surfaces, enabling a seamless blend of visual and LiDAR technology to improve detection, depth reconstruction, and spatial mapping. This brief introduction outlines key methods for analyzing LiDAR data, spanning from basic processing to complex recognition and task execution, while also discussing the points cloud formats and the LiDAR point distribution models. Further topics cover the derivation of geometric attributes such as surface normals, curvature, and spatial transformations, alongside discussions on point clouds classification, segmentation, and multi-object tracking. Finally, this brief overview delves into advanced areas of research, including physics inversion, texture propagation, and event-based systems.

Building on previously established findings, we extend our analysis to random fields that evolve independently at each point and maintain a uniform distribution as they evolve between discrete time intervals on the two-dimensional sphere. Building on these initial observations, we extend our analysis to encompass a broader class of stagnant random fields that have the property of being symmetric around the mean and then derive explicit recurrence relationships for the probability of reaching a specified state at a later time, given that the specified state has been met at an earlier time, with the condition that this relationship holds for the two-dimensional sphere when the relevant probabilities are finite.

The connection between neutrinos and cosmic rays at ultra-high energies and their possible relationship with each other and dark matter remains elusive due to limited data on neutrinos and the unknown nature of dark matter. This work presents research into the potential relationship between neutrinos and ultra-high-energy cosmic rays and contributes to constraining dark matter. The study involves analyzing neutrino events and calculating the probability of finding one or more neutrinos near the location of high-energy cosmic rays within a specified distance and time. It also simulates the decay of dark matter located within galactic centers and spiral arms to see if it can produce the observed associations. Findings show that neutrino interactions with ultra-high-energy cosmic rays remain within statistical fluctuations, while results for dark matter in form of supersymmetric gluballs and decaying dark matter in general align with observations.

We measure the friction within liquid foams using creep tests and find it is affected by the texture of the underlying monolayer. The friction is observed to be directly proportional to the surface viscosity, but the way viscosity changes with viscosity has two distinct patterns. When the viscosity varies discretely, the friction follows a linear pattern, yet in other cases, it is described by a square root. This non-linear relationship is believed to be caused by the simultaneous occurrence of viscous flow and a first-order yield stress solid phase within the foam.

This report focuses on using a series of convolutional neural networks to classify images in six categories from the ISIC data sets, encompassing benign and malignant tumors, as well as three other skin disease categories. We employed three different versions of CNNs, namely ResNet-50, InceptionV3, and NasNetMobile, and trained them on a dataset consisting of 8 skin disease categories. The models were capable of accurately distinguishing between the diseases, and NasNetMobile demonstrated the highest overall accuracy. To address a limitation of deep learning methods-skin biopsy-we developed a novel approach to identify samples with unusual characteristics by analyzing the decision vectors produced by the trained networks, and applying unsupervised learning techniques to these vectors. Ultimately, we discovered that using clustering and outlier detection techniques on the vectors allowed us to effectively identify samples that were similar to healthy moles and melanomas.

Investigating the side branch instability in a rotating Hele-Shaw cell is valuable in understanding and developing centrifugal pumps, as well as enhancing our knowledge of fingering patterns caused by a high-velocity jet impinging on a liquid surface under rotation. A jet of fluid, under the influence of a vertical angular velocity, was studied as it impacts a pool of the same liquid and causes an intricate side branch instability. A vertical jet was created using a precision syringe pump within a rotating Hele-Shaw cell. Under specific conditions of rotation and viscosity, the instability resulted in a pattern of branches that expanded in both radius and area. We were able to measure the thickness of these branches as they grew. A theoretical model was developed incorporating surface tension, viscosity, and rotational forces to explain the complexity of this phenomenon.

The code found a good match between 18 to 33 GHz, with a relative abundance of cyc-C5H3(CCC) greater than 10^-9. In neural machine translation, current modeling techniques for next token probability may lack sufficient information, potentially leading to overgenerated elements. To address this limitation, we introduce an innovative strategy that enables the model to consider elements that will be generated subsequently, thereby aligning more closely with target language construction rules. By incorporating look-ahead constraints on previously generated elements and introducing corresponding loss functions, we enhance the coherence between sequential elements. Experimentation on the News Translator dataset demonstrates the effectiveness of this technique in correcting overgeneration issues and improving model performance by 8 F1 points in back-translation direction and 5 points in primary translation direction, also facilitating better model cycle consistency.

Computing systems are complex and characterized by numerous constraints, including limited resources, unpredictable patterns, and varying demands. This paper argues for a flexible framework for designing and developing computational frameworks that account for these complexities. Through the example of the Grid, the design process is explored from its early stages to its current state, highlighting the significance of creating abstract models that simplify the intricacies of underlying hardware and software components. Furthermore, it suggests that innovation can be achieved by building modular components that adhere to specific design principles, allowing them to be reused and adapted for different applications.

In this study, we develop a Dissipative Unified Dark Fluid Model, combining dark energy and matter into a single entity. By applying conservation laws to this model, we derive a key equation that influences the model's evolution. This equation has solutions that can be either expanding or contracting, depending on the initial conditions. A key outcome of this research is the discovery that the model's phase space consists of two distinct regions, each representing an expanding or contracting behavior. These regions are connected by a boundary known as the Cauchy horizon, which separates them. The most significant discovery is that the region of the phase space corresponding to the same behavior as its precursor can be reached without a Big Bang or Big Crunch event, but rather through a smooth transition known as a Big Bounce. This concept aligns with recent theories of quantum gravity, which eliminate the possibility of singularities. Furthermore, this model can be mathematically described using a damped pendulum equation, which has solutions consisting of coherent-like oscillations whose amplitude decreases due to dissipation, ultimately settling into a stable equilibrium. The equation of this equilibrium corresponds to a critical Seiberg-Witten curve, which has been shown to describe the equation of dark energy in other models.

Understanding curiosity in learners within science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) learning contexts remains a significant challenge due to its intangible nature. Curiosity drives learners to engage with their learning environment, interact with peers, and actively participate in stem learning. Nevertheless, there is still much research needed to develop effective methods and tools for assessing curiosity within multimodal learning environments. This study proposes a novel approach, combining modalities, to evaluate curiosity activity levels during collaborative learning. By utilizing modalities including verbal interactions, facial expressions, and movement patterns, we created a model and validated it through empirical testing. Our results indicate that motion sensor data, when integrated with audio and video modalities, can accurately assess curiosity activity levels in learners. Contrary to our expectations, the addition of more sensor modalities did not necessarily enhance model performance. Therefore, a multimodal system consisting of Microsoft Surface tablets, inertial motion sensors, and a motion-sensing lamp can effectively evaluate curiosity in groups of learners.

Gaussian process models have been successfully applied to nearby data using a covariance matrix, but their application to data on a graph is limited due to the lack of flexible models that incorporate both graph and metric information, as well as allow for models with finite support. This research introduces a new distribution, the Mat\'ern gamma graph process, which provides a flexible framework by combining elements of Mat\'ern coefficients, gamma distributions, and a RBF kernel, ultimately enabling the development of a flexible Laplacian regression model with a covariance matrix. Our results demonstrate that our approach maintains the same convergence rates as the standard Mat\'ern model while allowing for a more flexible description of data, outperforming the graph-based Gaussian regression model in terms of performance. Furthermore, an iterative conditional mode algorithm is proposed for graph-based mat\'ern regression, which has been shown to provide a significant performance improvement of up to nine times faster than the alternative.

Detecting road networks efficiently often relies on observing the movement of vehicles, but the challenges of data privacy and incomplete information necessitate a method using only aggregated and minimal vehicle trajectory information. To accomplish this, we propose an observability framework capable of determining precisely which roads can be effectively monitored by a fleet of ridesourcing vehicles under various urban traffic scenarios. Our approach includes a method to optimize vehicle movement, aiming to maximize the detectability of the road network while respecting real-world constraints such as traffic patterns and company policies. We demonstrate the practicality of our approach through detailed analyses and numerical examples, including an examination of network connectivity as roads are closed and the robustness of the detection process in response to fluctuations in the number of available vehicles. Our results indicate that the proposed vehicle scheduling method leads to high detectability of the network, maintains good connectivity even when up to three times the closed roads are removed, and steadily increases detection rates as vehicle fleets expand.

Neutrino and dark matter interactions with conventional matter are extremely weak, characterized by effective field theories with high-dimensional operators. By analyzing limits on $J/\psi$ decay into visible gamma rays and invisible particles, researchers can establish more stringent constraints than those set by direct experiments or neutrino oscillation studies. This provides valuable insights into the substructure of these field theories. The studies considered various theoretical frameworks, such as type-III dark sectors and neutrino magnetic moments, leveraging $J/\psi$ decay data to derive precise constraints. The researchers utilized $J/\psi$ decay statistics from the BESIII collaboration to formulate more accurate bounds, which can be integrated into global analyses of these phenomena.

Previous variable stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods have already been implemented using the stepsize doubling technique, and this work extends this work by directly optimizing these methods, and introducing a set of constraints to ensure order conditions are met; furthermore, theoretical analysis proves that direct optimization approaches lead to methods with consistent local steps of $p$-th order, and numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of these newly developed methods.

Multivariate functional time series analysis has gained significant interest in recent years. In this paper, we adapt the multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis framework to such data and investigate its performance across various dimensional domains, including unit, infinity, and countable sets. Theoretical proof establishes the framework's consistency and practical applications are demonstrated via simulation and real data examination, utilizing heart rate variability data.

Recent advancements in automated emotional sensing technologies (AES) have sparked significant interest. Yet, the capabilities of AES systems remain relatively unknown due to the scarcity of extensive evaluations across diverse evaluations. Some studies suggest that neural network-based AES systems exhibit significant inaccuracies when dealing with complex emotions. Building on this knowledge, our research investigates both decision support AES systems and direct mapping AES systems, discovering that they are prone to extreme sensitivity and unbalanced performance due to several underlying causes, including class discrepancies, varying label lengths, and uneven data distribution. Notably, we discover that these systems' vulnerabilities stem from their inability to accurately process nuanced emotional inputs.

The classic one-dimensional simple random walk was analyzed in relation to its local times. A notable observation made by D. Revuz in 1978 during a conference in Nice was the ease with which various asymptotic properties of local times could be understood through a probabilistic lens. A key insight was that the almost sure behavior of the random walk at time n largely determines the almost sure behavior of the scaled local times when conditioned on n. This paper builds on Revuz's work by establishing new results, specifically proving the global persistence of the set of times where the one-dimensional random walk local time is equal to its global minimum. A key outcome of this study is a new proof of a theorem by A. Dembo in 2001 regarding the Hausdorff dimension of the set of times where the local times equal a local minimum minimum.

Plasma must be accurately measured and modeled before effective control can be achieved.  Obtaining control over a plasma source is challenging due to its complex and nonlinear behavior, making it difficult to predict how the plasma will respond to certain adjustments.  In this study, key parameters of a plasma were measured using various diagnostics, including microwave interference, langmuir probes, bolometers, and optical diagnostics, as the plasma's density changed.  A set of equations was then applied to determine the plasma's characteristics, but it was found that these predictions matched the actual measurements only when the plasma was operating in a specific state known as the "helicon regime."  This discovery confirmed that this particular plasma regime is stable and reliable.  Furthermore, this finding allowed for the development of a control strategy specifically tailored to this plasma regime, which will allow for the effective creation of stable plasmas, a crucial requirement for the successful treatment of fusion-relevant plasmas.

In order to accelerate the degradation of microbial pesticides, chemical accelerators are employed to reduce their efficacy and prolong their safety for human consumption. This study integrates this knowledge into a microbial pesticide model by introducing a suppression term into its equation. A thorough analysis encompasses the model's key properties, equilibrium points, stability assessments, a bifurcation analysis, and statistical validation. Additionally, this research introduces an implicit scheme for generating accurate numerical solutions, along with corresponding graphical illustrations.

WW-Net is a novel WW-mask segmentation network designed to tackle tasks of medical image analysis and histopathology image segmentation.  The conventional mask-based approaches using fully supervised training have shown limited performance due to the scarcity of precise annotation data and extensive computation requirements for generating such annotations.  Our proposed WW-Net adopts a distinct two-step strategy to mitigate these issues, combining single-point sampling for precise nucleus localization with masked region sampling within the vicinity of identified nuclei for efficient and accurate WW-mask generation in less-computed time.  The network exhibits superior performance on challenging medAIA and PANDA datasets, showing significant reductions in errors and considerable improvements in F1-scores compared to state-of-the-art methods.  Moreover, the WW-NET model demonstrates streamlined training duration and substantially decreased computational requirements, facilitating its application on lower-performance hardware systems.

In the context of local class field theory, we tackle the issue of computing the local epsilon factor for certain cubic character sums within additive and multiplicative characters within specific groups defined by special orthogonal and symplectic types, where the characteristic of the underlying field is not two. For characters that are generic, we establish the necessary determinacy for these symbols and derive recursive relationships, thereby enabling the calculation of these symbols for a vast majority of cases.

Wernisch previously defined a graph G as having a hamiltonian path index tau(G) equal to the number of times one must apply the operation of creating a repeated graph until a hamiltonian path is achieved in the resulting repeated graph. This concept was later expanded upon by Song, who defined a graph G as being n-w hamiltonian if it possesses a repeated graph R_k (G) that is traceable for a specific integer R_k (G)=n with the smallest possible value of n being equal to tau(G). Additionally, Song established that if a graph G is 2-w hamiltonian and has an odd number of vertices, then its repeated graph R_2 (G) is either 1-w or 2-w hamiltonian, and if G is 3-w hamiltonian and has an odd number of vertices, then its repeated graph R_3 (G) is 1-w or 2-w hamiltonian, and if G is 4-w hamiltonian and has an odd number of vertices, then its repeated graph R_4 (G) is 1-w or 2-w or 3-w hamiltonian. This work extends the work of Wernisch and Song by proving that if a graph G is 5-w hamiltonian and has an odd number of vertices, then its repeated graph R_k (G) is 1-w or 2-w or 3-w or 4-w or 5

Cell death due to pyroptosis, triggered by SARS-CoV-2, can cause a build-up of this dead cell material that clogs airways and worsens the symptoms of the disease. This research develops a single-cell mathematical model, at the subcellular level, to simulate the molecular processes leading to pyroptosis during SARS-CoV-2 infection. The existing death rate models based on the balance between pro-caspase-1 and its converted form, do not accurately reflect pyroptotic cell lysis. Our single-cell death rate equation takes the necessary step of including the time required for the complete conversion of pro-caspase-1 to mature caspase-1 during pyroptosis. An analysis of human lung adenocarcinoma cell dynamics, specifically the A549 cells, during their pyroptotic process, led to estimates of the rates and initial amounts of key molecules, which were further validated via phase plane analysis and a comparison with experimental data. Using this model, various treatment scenarios with anti-inflammatory drugs, such as IL-1Ra, IL-18Ra, and acetylserine, were modeled to identify effective combinations that can prevent cell lysis. The outcomes of these simulations provide a clear criteria for the desired responses in the concentrations of critical molecules as well as their phosphorylated forms, which can serve as a foundation for designing successful clinical trials.
